- So what is a good way
to describe the workflow,

and how that requirements
checking is automated
within the Requirements & Systems Portal?
- I mean, of course,

we want to streamline the
workflow of engineers;
that that's the whole purpose
of the Requirements & Systems Portal
and also of A365, right?

And we always talk about
these three main benefits
or three main values, which is,

first, faster time to
market, so iterating faster,
then it's getting it the first time right,
So less errors, and also more innovation.
(light music)

- Hello everyone, and welcome
to the Altium OnTrack Podcast.
I'm your host, Zach Peterson.
Today we're talking with Louise Linblad,
VP of Product for Systems Engineering,
and Goncalo Ivo,

Head of Product for
Requirements & Systems Portal,
both here at Altium.
I'm very happy to be talking to them both

about the new Requirements
& Systems Portal app.

You all may remember the
Valispace acquisition.
This is related to that.
And this is a new product

that's going to be
available in Altium 365.

So I am very happy to be
talking to them both today.

Louise, Goncalo, thank you
so much for joining me.
- Thank you. Great to be here.

- So when we last looked
at requirements management,

Louise, I believe you were
on the podcast at that time,
we talked about the Valispace acquisition.

So what has happened
since the acquisition,

and how has that morphed
into this new tool
for requirements management?
- Sure, yeah, So we were on this podcast,
me and Marco, I believe, a few months ago,
when Valispace had just been acquired.
And I mean, just to recap a bit,
So Valispace was really acquired

to bring that requirements
and system engineering context
into the Altium products.
And basically having that way of...

So requirements is usually
where you start a project,

so where you actually
describe what you want to do,
how you want to build something,

and what are the needs
for the project, right?
And that part, kind of piece of the puzzle

was missing a bit in A365
and in the Altium products.

And that's really why Valispace
came in as an acquisition,

to connect that requirements
part to the detailed design.
And that connection is very powerful.
And I remember we talked last time

about this "one plus one is
more than two" vision, right?
So the more apps we have on the platform

and the more we connect
these things together,

the more powerful this
will be for users, right?

And basically, that vision
is still true, right?
So we wanted to,
we wanted A365 as a platform
to be like all the way from an idea
to manufacturing, basically,

so all connecting all
those tools together.

And basically what's happened
in the last nine months

is that we've really integrated
Valispace as a product,
and also the team, into Altium,

and integrated the product
as an app on Altium 365.
So now, as you introduced,

Goncalo had a product for
Requirements & Systems Portal.
We've rebranded also the app.
So now it's gonna be called,

it is called Requirements &
Systems Portal on Altium 365.
And our teams have worked very, very hard

in the last nine months
to make this happen.
And it's a really big milestone,
both for Altium, for Valispace as a team,
and also for our customers,

because we we're already
selling this now to customers,

and we've had the first
few ones coming in;
and it's very exciting to see

how we can help customers
across that full journey.
So we're very happy
for the work that everyone has put in,
both from our side, from Altium side
in the last nine months,
and now we can really see

that "one plus one is more
than two" coming to life.
So that's very exciting.

- Now, I think what's
interesting about this,

just kind of looking at a
higher-level view with Altium 365,

is that this is one of the
apps that's available on 365.
And there are actually multiple apps now.
Goncalo, if you could,

maybe tell us what that
experience is like for users

and what kinds of apps
they can access on 365,
not just with Requirements and Systems,

but in addition to
Requirements and Systems.

- Well, nowadays, the
Requirements & Systems Portal,
like we said, is one of the apps,
one of the first, I'll call it,
primary apps within A365.

But there's another one
which is, I would say,

the first of it, and the
one that's mostly used,
which is the BOM Portal.

That's a good example
of other applications

or native applications within
A365 or or Z Search data

where users can then search
for procurement data.
Those are the kind of hubs

that we will try to
expand the platform on.

But requirements and the
Requirements & Systems Portal,

the main thing why we created
as an app, in a sense,

is like it's to give the
users a unified experience,
let's call it like this,

that everything is between
one single environment
and with one single digital thread
so that users don't feel
that they are always working, connected,

not only between themselves
and within the same team,

but also with other teams
and other stakeholders.
So it's not just for electronic engineers,
it'll be for everyone that is involved
on the old product development life cycle.
So that's the main idea,

is that we then also enlarge
the application database.
And you can already go to altium365.com,

and you'll see there
the other available apps
and even the coming-soon apps,
they'll be described there.
- Now, when we talk about requirements
and requirements management, let's say,
I think, for a lot of companies,

they have a huge range of
different processes that they use.
So I'm wondering if you both could tell us
how would Altium 365 users

normally run these types of
requirements management tasks,
and how does that all change

with the new Requirements
& Systems Portal?
- Yeah, interesting, that's your question,
you make that question,
because we have collected data

either from Altium users
and even some webinars
and research on the data,
and like you said,

most of the users do
requirements management,
or at least even,

not even sometimes the
requirement management part,
but even needing to consider requirements

or taking consideration
of the requirements
while they're designing.

This is if we talk about
electronical engineers.
But they are doing it mostly,

almost like 30 to 50% do
it in Excel or spreadsheets
or other just loose-text tools like Notes,
or even just placing notes on the design.

That was also something
that usually came up.

Or using other tools
that are not so strong

on the requirements
management, like, for example,
task management tools, let say Jira.

And then there's a small
percentage that already uses,
or on the company, that they already have

a stricter process of
requirements management
using other already proper tools

like DOORS, Jama, or even
Valispace and others.
But the main thing is that all of these,

it's still a little bit
disconnected from the reality

and lots of data that comes
in the way of communication.
And what you're trying to bring
with the Requirements & Systems Portal
is that since the requirements

and the life on the
requirement life cycle,

it will be closer and
and directly connected
to the electronical engineer life cycle,

so available, I won't say on
the fly or while designing.
The idea that we reduce the gaps

for mixed communication
and wrong data sharing.
So that will be the idea
that the Requirements & Systems Portal

will bring into the world of
the electronical engineers.

- Yeah, I think a lot of
companies will maintain
like a master document
that has a list of requirements in it,

but it could be so long that
nobody wants to read it.
So maybe there's one person that knows
what all the requirements actually are,

and it's usually the
author of that document.

And then that document
doesn't have any connection
into the CAD tools.
So is it fair to say
that the Requirements & Systems Portal
kind of pulls out the individual pieces
of those big documents,
and then provides that connection
into the CAD project via 365?
Is that an okay way to describe this?
- Yeah, so that's one way to describe it.

But Requirements & Systems
Portal is more than just,

you know, putting the
documents and pieces together.

It's really a whole system for
managing your requirements.

So it's not only a place where
the requirements are stored;

it's actually where you
can have the traceability
of the history, who changed what,

where you can actually track
the status of the verification.

So it has a lot more things
than just being a document.
And on top of that comes of course
all the collaboration features, right?

So all that, everyone is
already used to an A365
that you can comment on requirements
where they actually are, right?

So you don't have to send
an email to someone asking
about some requirements.

You can actually comment on
them in the platform itself.
So all these things definitely are brought
with their Requirements & Systems Portal.

- So what is a good way
to describe the workflow

and how that requirements
checking is automated
within the Requirements & Systems Portal?
- Yeah, we always,
I mean, of course we want to streamline
the workflow of engineers;
that's the whole purpose
of the Requirements & Systems Portal
and also of A365, right?

And we always talk about
these three main benefits
or three main values,
which is first faster time to market,
so iterating faster,
then it's getting it the first time right,

so less errors, and also
more innovation, right?

So just to go through
them a bit more in detail,
what you mentioned,
that there might be one person
that knows about all the requirements,

but it's not shared across
the different departments,

it's not shared across the
engineers that are working on it,

this kind of limited
visibility on the requirements
is really a problem,

because you might design
something for weeks
without knowing that a requirement changed
or that there was even a requirement

that you were supposed
to follow from the start.
I think it's an interesting answer
also from the survey that we sent out,
that Goncalo mentioned,
that there are a lot of people
that said they never saw a requirement
in the design process, which is a problem,

because then what are you
designing against, right?
So you need to have some kind of notion

or some kind of visibility on
what those requirements are
and what you're designing against.

So when these things are
misunderstood or misinterpreted,

it costs a lot of money
and it costs a lot of time.
So what we wanna try to achieve

is that you can iterate
faster on these things
and actually have more collaboration
between the different kinds of engineers
that are working on this, right?
And then the second thing
is getting it right the first time, right?

So what costs a lot of money
and time is errors, right?
It's very difficult to measure

how much an error or how
much an inconsistent value

or an inconsistent
requirement actually costs,

because you usually discover
it very late in the process.
But we want to shift that a bit
so that you can actually,
like, if all the data is connected
and if you can, for example,

connect which requirements
are applicable to which design
and where these requirements were verified
or where they were implemented,

you will be able to get
it right the first time
and not have to redo it a million times
because there were these kind of problems
or miscommunications.

And of course, if you
do both of those things
and engineers have more time to do
what they were actually hired to do,
to do the engineering part

and not actually try to look
up requirements and documents,

then you get this more innovative
kind of way of working.
So instead of being afraid to make changes
because you don't know what the effect is,
if everything is connected,
you can start experimenting more,

you can start making changes
and seeing the effects
that a certain change will have

on the rest of your process
or the rest of your design.
So it really makes it,

it even makes your
organization more innovative,

because you have more time
to do those kind of things.
- So one thing I'm in anxious to see

is to see a demo of this
new new app on Altium 365.

I think, Goncalo, you've got
something prepared for us.
- Yes, sure, I'll give it a go.
- [Zach] Okay, I see we're live.

And so just for everyone
that is listening on audio,
you've got a few different windows
pulled up in your browser.

One of them is the
Requirements Manager Portal.

It looks here like you have
a big list of requirements.
And then I see that you have

a project pulled up in Altium
365 in your other windows.
- [Goncalo] Yes, I'll try to show first.

The first thing is the
Requirements & Systems Portal app,
which is accessible through a direct link,
or even, as we can see here,
while navigating from the workspace
so that it could be,
it's here on the nine-dots menu,

it's an application, so
we can navigate here.
And what we are seeing here is already
let's say a full list of requirements,
which can be, just like you said,
the first list that the project manager
or the system engineer provides
to what is the requirement
that a board in a way needs to comply to
when you're designing a board.
Here I expressed,
because the Requirements & Systems Portal
is currently used and it can be used

for more than just
electronic requirements,

it can be used on the full
development life cycle.

So the example that we have
here, it's doing a full drone.

And for the full drone you will
have subsets of requirements
which go from higher-level requirements
for the drone itself.

Then they can be
decomposed and lowered down
into product power requirements,

flight requirements that
can go down to, for example,

to the motherboard that
you need to design,

or to the flight management
unit that you need to design
as an electronical engineer.

Those can then be assigned
to what we call a block
within the RSP.
So we can say that this block
should follow this subset of requirements.
This can be set by the system engineer,

or it can also be the electronical
engineer that says, okay,

to implement these
requirements or this board,
I need to do X, Y, Z.
And then you can trace that.
But then, I'll say,

this is the first part
of the process in a way,
which is, okay, what are the requirements

that I need to follow or
that I'm designing against.

But then comes the connection
to the electronic world

or the deep connection
that we're trying to build;

which is when we define this
block as a type of electronics,

and then we can do the
linking between, okay,
this block and this set of requirements

to the project that I'm
building in AD or in A365,
which is what we call Altium Dream.
And when we perform this, there's already,

for the Requirements
& Systems Portal side,

there's already two
things that will happen.
One is we'll have just a quick review
of what we have already designing
or designing on the electronical side.

But the second one, and
which is more interesting

and goes also to a point
that you mentioned before
around automatic verification,
which is when we do this deep connection,

it's not only exposing
requirements on the Altium 365
or on AD that also, on a few seconds,
but it's also pulling back data
and information from the design.

In this case it's pulling the
main properties of the design.
For example, the number of layers
or even the minimum/maximum trace width
that are currently on that Altium project.
- [Zach] Here you have a list of objects.
I see here Blind via count, for example.

You mentioned, you know,
minimum and maximum trace width.
It's actually pulling in objects
from the Altium Designer PCB doc file.

And so now the Requirements
& Systems Portal
can see objects in your PCB doc

and then compare that
against some specification
that you've set up here
in the Requirements & Systems Portal.
- Yeah, as an example,

so if we have, this is
a simplistic example,
but if we have a requirement
that we shouldn't design a board
with more than seven layers, correct?
But if you're not aware,
by getting this automatic number of layers
or other values from in,
we can automatically check
if you are fulfilling your design or not
with the simple, with the simple,
with the simple mathematical rule,

we can directly validate if
this is being fulfilled or not

and warn the user if it's
feel failing or deviating
from this requirement.
This is one.

But then on the Altium
side or on the A365 side,
I'll show part of it on AD
and part of it on ADC side, the web part.

These requirements that I
assigned to these projects,
so we can see they will be accessible
to what we call the requirements panel.

And while you are navigating
on the requirements panel,

you can see the context
of the requirements
and what are those requirements.
And then there are,
I'll say three main actions

that are available for
the electronical engineer

while designing with the
requirements on context,
which is placing the requirement.
So you'll say, okay,
this was the place or the location
where I've implemented this requirement.
The other one is to task someone to do it.

So we can easily create
a task to someone else.
And then we can see always, okay, where,

and navigate to where are those
requirements placed or not
or where are they tasked.

And the third one, which is
the electronical engineer,
can also directly contribute

to the validation and
verification of that requirement,

because it can directly
set the status of those
or of the validation of those requirements

from within the Altium
environment or AD or A365.

And then that will be
directly reflected here

on the validation activities
or that are defined on the RSP.
On the other way, a system engineer
doesn't need to to always probe, in a way,
the electronical engineer,
like, is my requirement fulfilled

or is my requirement being
considered or implemented?
Because each time an electronical engineer
places a requirement,
there's also here the design references
that allows for the system engineer

or other electronical
engineers to directly navigate
to the place on the design where,
to the location on the design
where this requirement was placed.

So this is all within the
same A365 environment,

where you can easily
navigate back and forward
between the applications,
be it web viewer, AD, or A365 or RSP.
- [Zach] Yeah, this is really interesting,
what you just did.
You had one of the requirements
tagging a specific schematic sheet,

and it just automatically
appears as a link
in the Requirements Manager.
Now, there's automatic validation,
but of course someone can then go through
and manually select this

and really validate it
deeper if they want to.

So it doesn't fully remove
the human from the loop.
- [Goncalo] Yeah, no, yes.

The human can always
take the final decision.

And now that you mentioned
that, for example,
even when writing the requirements,
we have some AI-assisted features
that can help you to create requirements

to flow down to better design
and write your requirements.
But even those AI features that we have,
we call the ValiAssistant,
which can help you to generate

or even improve your requirements
or give you suggestions
to further break down the requirements.
But even that, it's always assistance.

So ultimately it's on the
user to take the decision,

and on the engineers to make
the final decision and choice.
- Since we've gotten to this point,

maybe one or both of you
could answer this question:

how long does it normally
take to go through
and define all of those requirements
inside the Requirements & Systems Portal?
And maybe how does that compare
to setting it up in some other system?
Or is that not really a valid comparison?

Because it sounds to me
like if you invest the time
in the Requirements & Systems Portal,

it saves you other review
time on the backend

by streamlining some of
that automated checking.

- For sure, I think there are
several points to this, right?
So one thing is what Goncalo just showed,
which is the AI functionalities, right?

We can actually help you
to create requirements
and to break them down.

So imagine you have a very
high-level need, right?

So you're making a drone
that should fly autonomously

and can fly for one hour
without being recharged, right?
That's a very high-level need.

And that would usually
take a system engineer
or a requirement engineer quite some time

to start breaking that down
and start thinking about, okay,
what are the subsystems that we need?
What are the solutions that we can do

for this kind of product
that we're building?

And we can actually help you
take that first step, right?
So as Goncalo said,
it's not about, you know,
making all the work for you
or making all the decisions for you,
but it's assisting in that part,
which some things are creative work,
some things are just finding values
in the requirements,

so that you don't have
to like manually check
that that value is correct,
but you can create these automatic rules.

So if you set it up well
from the start, let's say,

with these kind of
connection to the design
and these kind of automatic validations
and set that up from the start,

then the process will
be much, much smoother
once you come to the end of it, right?

So I think those are
probably the main two things,
that we can help you to get started,

to do the first steps
and to check actually
that like you are actually
breaking the requirements down correctly,

that there are no inconsistencies
in these kind of things,

but also then help you to
do that automatic validation

so that you don't have
to manually go and check
in all the documents
and make sure that everything is correct
and everything is consistent.

But the system will basically
tell you, like, hey,
there is a problem here, go look at this.

Or everything is green, that
you can move forward, right?
So it definitely
helps being faster with what you're doing,

to set it up in a good
system from the start.
- And if I may add,

for those 30 to 50% that
already have the requirements
either on Word or already on Excel,

the Excel can be directly
imported to the RSP.

So it's just a drag and
drop of of the Excel,
which you can then start,
you won't start from scratch.
So you just put it on the tool.

It'll be in a matter of
minutes to set it up,
link it to a block,
and then have it available on,
so that you can then start
having the traceability you need
to write, copy and paste from, or do that.

So it's just a simple import
on that functionality.
- Very cool.

That's actually something
I was going to ask.

Can you drop your Word
document into the system,

and it pulls out all the
individual requirements.

- The Word is trickier because
Word depends on formatting,
but we can also help on do that,

and we've been helping
customers to upload that.

But the Excel, it's almost
like straightforward.
- Okay. Okay.
Another question I have here,

just going back and
looking at some of the list
of basic requirements, again,

you showed things like Blind
via count and Trace width.

What other objects can the
system pull from a PCB doc file?

Can it pull reference designators,
net names, net classes?
Can it pull specific design rule values,
those kinds of things?

- Well, for now, it's only
pulling the project data.

So the project definition data
that's assigned to a project.

So this is the first step of
what we want to show customers,
driving a new direction that we're going.

But we want to go and to
continue on this data sharing,
because once RSP is within the platform,
on Altium 365 platform,

we will empower it and enable
it to connect to more data
that detects on the tools.
So be it net data, like you mentioned,
or even going as low as the BOM properties
so that you can...
The long-term vision is if you can say,
let's say that you have a requirement
that says that you cannot select
or that all your board proper,

all your board components
should be within a range
of minus 20 to plus 55 degrees.

So if we can pull that data
directly from your components
when you're selecting your components

or you know about it, this
is what we want to achieve.

And this is what we feel
that it will be beneficial

for everyone on the loop, be
it the electronical engineer,
the procurement engineer,

or ultimately the person
that is receiving the board.

So because you'll be
able to design faster,

catch errors faster, and
ultimately provide value faster.

- Yeah, that sounds like it
would be able to maybe leverage
the Z2 data integration,

and then check against that
kind of data coming in from Z2.
- Yeah, that's the long-term vision.
- Speaking of the long-term vision,
what else is in the future
for Requirements & Systems Portal?

I mean, I get, you know,
expanding the objects
that you can see inside of a PCB doc,
but what else is there?
- That's one of it, it's those parts.
The other one is also to try to link it

to what we call more standards
and type requirements,
the things that are more common

to the industry of the
electronical agencies.

So it's the type to keep
continuing to tailoring it
to do the electronics use case.
This is on the RSP side.
And then on the full requirements

within the ecosystem
and on the environment,

Louise can also share a little
bit more on what's to come.

- Yeah, for sure, I think one
is making the RSP app better.
And as Goncalo said,

like, connecting it more
deeply into Altium and A365.
And the other part

is having that traceability
of requirements
across all apps of the platform, right?
Because requirements is not something

that you just do in the
start of the project, right?

It's not you have an idea,
you do all the requirements,
and then you start your design.
It's really a bit like zigzagging
between requirements and design, right?
So you have your high-level requirements,
and then you start your system design;
then you have more requirements

depending on the subsystems
that you're choosing;
then you refine the requirements
when you go down into the design details.
And then as you go up,

you also have manufacturing
requirements, et cetera, right?

So it's not about
Requirements & Systems Portal
as an app is great,

but also kind of expanding
that context of requirements
across the whole Altium ecosystem,

because requirements
really gives that context
to what you're trying to build.

And then we can start
becoming smarter, right?

We can start being better
at assisting the engineers

and helping the engineers
taking better decisions,

because we know what
they are trying to build
and what they are building against,
let's say the stakeholder requirements.

And then we can start
really helping engineers

to make sure that they are
going in the right direction
and doing it faster, right?

So really, I think helping
engineers making better decisions
is by having that requirement context
is really the ultimate goal.
- Well, as all of this stuff unfolds
and the app develops and matures,

of course we would love
to have you both come back
and tell us all about it.

And hopefully we'll get
some folks who sign up
and start using this thing.
Where can interested users go

to learn about the
Requirements & Systems Portal?

Should we send them over
to 365 or altium365.com?

- Yes, I'll say that will be
the main one, altium365.com.
And if they go to also explore more
a little bit of the features

already on the documentation
side of Altium 365,

they can already see mostly
this part of the integration,
how this would play out on both tools,
on both AD and on the web viewer of A365.
- Excellent.

Well, Louise, Goncalo,
thank you both so much
for joining us today.
- Thank you, Zach.
- Thank you, Zach, for having us.
- Thank you.

To everyone that's out there
watching and listening,
We've been talking with Louise Linblad,
VP of Product Systems Engineering,
and Goncalo Ivo,

Head of Product for
Requirements & Systems Portal.
If you're watching on YouTube,
make sure to hit the Like button
and hit the Subscribe button.
You'll be able to keep up

with all of our podcast
episodes and tutorials
as they come out.

And last but not least,
don't stop learning,

stay on track, and
we'll see you next time.
Thanks, everybody.
(light music)

title: Automating Requirements: How Altium 365 is Changing Engineering
